tour.title: Project Overview and Entry Point
tour.description: The package root great_expectations/__init__.py is where the tour starts: it sets the version, imports core submodules in dependency order, and promotes get_context, Checkpoint, ExpectationSuite, ResultFormat, RunIdentifier and ValidationDefinition to the top-level gx namespace. It also registers core metrics and expectations, so importing the package wires up the whole registry-driven framework. The version module sits beside it and derives the package version from git metadata.
tour.languageLesson: Python package __init__ files act as barrels: re-exporting names with 'from .x import Y' defines the public API, and importing a module only for its side effects (as done here for registration) is a common plugin-registry pattern.

tour.title: Foundation: Decorators, Exceptions, Constants
tour.description: Shared building blocks used everywhere live at the package root. _docs_decorators marks symbols as public API and appends deprecation or version-added notes to docstrings, exceptions.py is the central catalogue of GX exception classes, and constants.py holds shared placeholders. These files have very high fan-in, so recognizing them now makes later steps easier to read.
tour.languageLesson: Python decorators are functions that wrap other callables or classes. Here they attach metadata (public API status, deprecation notices) to symbols and rewrite docstrings at import time.

tour.title: Compatibility Shims
tour.description: The compatibility package isolates optional third-party libraries (pandas, pyspark, sqlalchemy, pydantic, typing_extensions) and their version differences behind thin modules. The README explains the folder's version-specific shim approach and file naming conventions. These shims have the highest fan-in in the graph, so the rest of the codebase imports these wrappers instead of the libraries directly.
tour.languageLesson: A compatibility shim wraps an optional import in try/except and exposes a placeholder or fallback when the library is missing, letting the rest of the code import the name unconditionally.

tour.title: Core Domain Model
tour.description: The core package holds the domain objects the framework builds on: ExpectationSuite (a named collection of Expectations), the ExpectationSuiteValidationResult types, Domain, MetricDomainTypes, ResultFormat and RunIdentifier. BatchDefinition ties a named partitioner to a data asset and builds batch requests. These types are the shared vocabulary for datasources, validators and renderers in later steps.
tour.languageLesson: Many of these models are pydantic classes: field type hints become runtime validation, and the same model drives serialization to and from JSON.

tour.title: Data Context: The Entry to Everything
tour.description: get_context in context_factory selects an ephemeral, file or cloud context, all of which derive from AbstractDataContext. The abstract context is the central object managing datasources, stores, suites and checkpoints. Building on the domain objects from Step 4, the concrete contexts decide where those objects live: in memory, as YAML on disk, or in GX Cloud.

tour.title: Stores and Factories
tour.description: Stores wrap a StoreBackend and translate keys and values between GX objects and serialized form, with specialized stores for expectation suites, validation definitions and checkpoints in file or Cloud backends. Factories such as the generic Factory base class provide add, delete, get and all access to these resources through the data context. Together they give the context a uniform CRUD layer over persistence.
tour.languageLesson: core/factory/factory.py defines a generic abstract base class; Python generics let one CRUD contract be reused across suites, checkpoints and validation definitions.

tour.title: Fluent Datasources and Batches
tour.description: The fluent datasource API describes data connections and data assets that produce batches. interfaces.py defines the abstract DataAsset, Datasource and Batch models, while concrete modules add pandas, Spark and SQL support. A fluent BatchRequest carries options, a batch slice and a partitioner, linking back to the BatchDefinition from Step 4.
tour.languageLesson: Fluent here means a builder-style API of add_* and read_* methods; the .pyi stub files declare the signatures of dynamically generated asset classes for type checkers.

tour.title: Execution Engines
tour.description: An ExecutionEngine loads batch data, resolves metric bundles and partitions domain kwargs. The Pandas, Spark and SQLAlchemy engines implement this for each backend, with matching BatchData wrappers. This abstraction is what lets the same Expectation run unchanged on a DataFrame or a SQL database.

tour.title: Metrics and Metric Providers
tour.description: Metrics compute facts about data, such as row counts, column maximums or null counts. MetricProvider and its metric_value and metric_partial decorators tag per-engine implementations, and the registry maps metric names to them; the newer metrics package defines a generic pydantic Metric base. Providers like column_max and column_values_null implement the same metric for pandas, SQLAlchemy and Spark.
tour.languageLesson: The metric_value decorator binds a method to an engine class (pandas, SQLAlchemy, Spark) so one metric name can have several backend-specific implementations.

tour.title: The Expectation Base and Built-in Catalog
tour.description: The Expectation base class is a pydantic model that declares what it checks, which metrics it needs and how it renders. Concrete expectations such as ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeNull and ExpectColumnMaxToBeBetween request metrics from Step 9 and judge the results. The core barrel re-exports every built-in expectation, and the schemas README documents how their JSON schemas are structured.
tour.languageLesson: Expectation uses a metaclass together with pydantic, so subclasses can register themselves when defined; this is why importing a module is enough to add its expectation to the catalog.

tour.title: Validator and Metric Dependency Graph
tour.description: The Validator binds an execution engine, an active batch and an expectation suite, then resolves the metrics each expectation needs. MetricConfiguration identifies a metric by name and domain kwargs, and the ValidationGraph orders metric computations by dependency. This runtime heart connects the engines, metrics and expectations from Steps 8 to 10.

tour.title: Validation Definitions and Checkpoints
tour.description: A ValidationDefinition links a BatchDefinition with an ExpectationSuite and runs validation to yield a suite result. A Checkpoint runs a list of ValidationDefinitions and then triggers ValidationActions such as Slack, Teams, PagerDuty or email notifications. These are the production-facing units that the stores from Step 6 persist.

tour.title: Rendering and Data Docs
tour.description: Renderers convert expectation configurations and validation results into prescriptive and diagnostic content, using RendererConfiguration and the Renderer base to look up render functions in the registry. SiteBuilder and page renderers assemble full Data Docs pages, and the Jinja views turn them into HTML. This closes the loop by making validation outcomes human readable.
tour.languageLesson: Jinja2 (.j2) templates mix HTML with {{ expressions }} and {% blocks %}; the Data Docs views compose small templates such as the top navbar and bootstrap table into pages styled by the default CSS.

tour.title: Profiling, Metric Repository, Self-Check
tour.description: Beyond the main validation path, the legacy profile package and the experimental metric repository gather statistics about data. BatchInspector runs MetricRetrievers against a batch and returns a MetricRun, which a DataStore can persist. The self_check utilities build validators and engines across many backends and support testing the framework itself.
